prompt: Write a short blog post about why everyone should grow something. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# Grow Something

Everyone should grow something; I hold this view with the calm of a man who has been wrong about tomatoes for years and has not let it affect his convictions. It does not matter much what the something is. A pot of basil on a windowsill will do, as will a row of peas, or a patch of turf, provided it is tended and not merely admired through the glass.

The first reason is that it corrects one's sense of proportion. A person who has watched a seed take nine days to produce two leaves will never again be impatient with a slow elevator. Nations are built in less time than it takes a squash to decide whether it intends to bear. The garden keeps its own calendar, and it does not consult yours.

The second reason is humility, which is a good thing to have and a difficult thing to acquire by other means. I have lined the ground, planted, hoed, and staked, and then watched a rabbit hold a private banquet at my expense. No lecture, however well delivered, has taught me as much about the limits of human planning as that rabbit. I bear him no ill will; he was thorough.

The third reason is the eating. It is a pleasure to eat of the fruit of one's own toil, if it be nothing more than a head of lettuce. A store-bought lettuce is a perfectly respectable vegetable, but it arrives without a history. Your own has one, and you know every chapter of it, including the part where you forgot to water it for a week and it forgave you anyway.

There is also the matter of the body, which was not designed to spend its days bent over a screen. A good hoe, used by an upright and reasonable person, does away with the necessity of the hinge in the back. An hour with one will leave you tired in a way that sitting never does; this is the honest sort of tired, and it improves the sleep considerably.

Finally, a garden gives one something to say to the neighbors. Conversation across a fence is a lost art, and zucchini is its last defender. Nobody has ever grown only one zucchini; the plant does not permit it. You will therefore be obliged to give some away, and in this fashion the whole street becomes acquainted.

So find a pot, or a corner, or a strip of ground that nobody is using. Put something in it and keep it alive. If it dies, you will have learned something; if it lives, you will have dinner. Either result is better than the one you get by staying indoors.
